After the Dormouse's story is repeatedly interrupted, Alice leaves and finally finds a route into the garden. There, card-shaped gardeners are painting white roses red to conceal an error. The King and Queen of Hearts arrive with their court. The Queen repeatedly demands executions and forces Alice into a croquet game played with flamingos, hedgehogs, and moving card-soldiers instead of normal equipment. The Cheshire Cat appears above the ground, creating an argument about whether a head without a body can be beheaded. Alice survives the Queen's anger as the game collapses into disorder.

The Duchess returns from custody and walks with Alice, finding morals in everything until the Queen drives her away. The Queen then sends Alice with the Gryphon to meet the Mock Turtle. The Mock Turtle gives a tearful account of his childhood, his school beneath the sea, and a curriculum built from distorted versions of ordinary subjects. He and the Gryphon describe and perform the Lobster Quadrille, then ask Alice about her adventures. Her attempts to repeat familiar verses again produce altered nonsense. Their songs and explanations are interrupted by the announcement that a trial is beginning, and the Gryphon rushes Alice back to the royal court.

The Knave of Hearts is tried for stealing the Queen's tarts, with the King acting as judge and a jury of animals struggling to write anything sensible. The Hatter, the Duchess's Cook, and Alice are called as witnesses. None supplies reliable evidence, and the court treats an unsigned poem as proof by assigning meanings it does not contain. Alice begins growing during the hearing and becomes confident enough to challenge the King's invented rules and the Queen's demand for punishment before a verdict. When the Queen orders her execution, Alice says the court is merely a pack of cards. The cards swarm over her, and she wakes beside her sister on the riverbank. She tells her sister the dream and runs home, while her sister reflects on the strange vision and Alice's future.

recaps.ending: The Gridgrad base and nearly completed viceregal palace formally open while the surrounding capital remains under construction. A rapid Escobaran plan for a local plazcrete factory has eased the project's critical supply problem. Cordelia continues her transition away from the viceregency, and Jole begins resigning from military service after refusing the Chief of Operations post on Barrayar. His replacement is expected within several months. Miles and his family leave Sergyar having accepted Cordelia and Jole as partners and Jole's prospective sons as members of Aral's family. Jole orders one of his three stored sons into gestation, while Cordelia's next child is also developing and Aurelia is part of their household. Construction has begun on Cordelia and Jole's shared home at Port Nightingale. Jole plans to enter graduate study in field biology after completing additional academic work, and the couple envision using a research vessel to investigate Sergyar's marine life. That scientific project remains prospective, but their commitment to a shared civilian life on Sergyar is firm.
recaps.in_short: Years after Aral Vorkosigan's death, Cordelia returns to Sergyar intending to leave the viceregency and raise daughters created from their stored reproductive material. She gives Oliver Jole, Aral's former partner, a related opportunity to have sons. Jole creates three viable embryos, begins a new relationship with Cordelia, and must choose between their emerging family life and promotion to Barrayar's Chief of Operations. Their relationship becomes public during a birthday picnic that ends in violence and a firestorm of native radials. Jole is burned while shielding Miles's children, then tells Miles about his history with Aral and the planned boys. Miles accepts them as family. Jole refuses the promotion, begins resigning his command, and starts one son's gestation. As Gridgrad's base and palace open, Cordelia and Jole build a home at Port Nightingale and plan a civilian future centered on family and marine research.

recaps.text: Previously: Cordelia was married to Aral Vorkosigan, a major Barrayaran military figure, and became the mother of Miles Vorkosigan. Cordelia later became Vicereine of Sergyar, where Oliver Jole rose to command the planet's military forces. Aral died before the events of this book. Cordelia and Jole begin the story as long-standing professional partners in Sergyar's civil and military leadership.

Cordelia returns to Sergyar carrying reproductive material preserved from her marriage to Aral. She intends to create as many as six daughters, use the surname Naismith to avoid inheritance disputes, and eventually retire as Vicereine. She also offers Jole a path to fatherhood using donated enucleated eggs and Aral's stored material. Jole completes the clinic's evaluation and creates four embryos, but one fails early. He freezes the remaining three while he considers whether he can combine parenthood with military command. Cordelia begins gestation of one of her own embryos and makes reciprocal guardianship plans with Jole. Meanwhile, the selected site for Sergyar's second base is Gridgrad, but deteriorating plazcrete delivered too early threatens its schedule. During a memorial trip, Cordelia and Jole discover teenagers stranded after their attempt to destroy native radials causes a fire. A later private sailing trip ends in shelter from a storm, where Jole and Cordelia acknowledge their attraction and begin an intimate relationship. They agree that it is a new bond between them, not simply a revival of what they once shared with Aral.

Cordelia and Jole continue their relationship privately while deciding whether discretion can last. Cordelia confirms that six embryos are viable and plans to leave office within a year. Jole confronts the practical demands of raising children, from housing and support to the limits imposed by his career. Cordelia informs Emperor Gregor and her close Barrayaran family circle about her retirement and daughters. Aurelia is already developing, with five sisters frozen. Miles, Ekaterin, and their children then arrive unexpectedly on Sergyar. Miles knows about the daughters but not Jole's three possible sons, whose origins would require revealing Jole's earlier relationship with Aral. Jole is offered the leading candidacy for Chief of Operations on Barrayar and realizes that accepting would conflict with both fatherhood and a life with Cordelia, who will remain on Sergyar. The Gridgrad project is still troubled by its plazcrete supply. During the visit, Cordelia tells Miles and Ekaterin that she and Jole are dating. Ekaterin is supportive, while Miles raises political and family concerns. He still does not know about the prospective sons, and Jole's career decision remains open.

Miles learns more difficult truths about Aral and begins to accept that his father's life cannot be reduced to an idealized image. The family tours Aral's mothballed flagship, where military history and the continuing danger of biological warfare reinforce the value of scientific expertise. Cordelia encourages Alex to choose a future other than the military path Miles favors. At the same time, the Gridgrad capital project remains exposed to a supplier's monopoly demands. Jole's relationship with Cordelia becomes known on the base, and his choice between Sergyar and the Chief of Operations post grows urgent. At his birthday picnic, the couple make their partnership publicly visible. Drunken players vandalize Mikos ghem Soren's cultural exhibit and assault members of its delegation before security intervenes. A bottle rocket then ignites a swarm of native radials. Jole shields Alex and Helen from the burning debris and suffers substantial burns. While recovering, he tells Miles that his long relationship with Aral later included Cordelia and explains that three embryos descended from Jole and Aral are stored for him. Miles accepts the prospective boys as half-brothers. Jole refuses the Barrayaran post and decides to support the Sergyar transition before resigning from service.

After the picnic disaster, Cordelia manages the public account of the emergency while preserving evidence of Jole's protection of her grandchildren. Mikos ghem Soren faces disgrace and removal by his consulate. After Kaya Vorinnis refuses his proposed marriage, he seeks asylum; Cordelia grants it on the condition that he work as a plumber on Sergyar. The men responsible for the assault face disciplinary consequences. Kareen Koudelka arrives with an Escobaran company able to erect a prefabricated plazcrete factory rapidly, giving the Gridgrad project a workable answer to its supply crisis. Miles departs with his family after affirming that Jole and the planned boys belong within the family. The new Gridgrad base and nearly complete viceregal palace open successfully, though the city remains under construction. Jole begins his resignation process and expects a replacement within two to six months. He directs his physician to begin gestation for one of his sons, while another of Cordelia's children is also in a uterine replicator. Cordelia and Jole are building a shared home at Port Nightingale. Jole turns toward graduate study in field biology, and they plan a future investigating Sergyar's marine biosphere together.

characters.description: An elderly classics master at St Oswald's Grammar School in Malbry, where he has taught for more than three decades. Straitley is irritable about administrative fashions and fiercely loyal to the old school, its pupils, and the Latin he teaches. His long memory for the institution makes him unusually alert to small inconsistencies when the new academic year begins to go wrong.
characters.name: Roy Straitley

characters.description: An unnamed narrator who has entered St Oswald's staff under a concealed identity. As the child of a former school porter, the narrator grew up excluded from the privileged world inside the school gates and now describes a deliberate campaign to injure the institution from within. The plan depends on disguise, patience, and knowledge of how rumors and minor rule-breaking can damage trust.
characters.name: The Black Pawn

characters.description: The headmaster of St Oswald's at the start of a difficult new term. Bishop must protect the school's reputation while managing worried parents, staff rivalries, new technology, and a series of incidents that initially appear unrelated.
characters.name: Pat Bishop

characters.description: A St Oswald's boy whom the young Snyde befriends years before the present-day attack on the school. Leon provides a route into the institution's private spaces and becomes central to the memories from which Snyde's grievance develops.
characters.name: Leon Mitchell

characters.description: The school porter and parent of the child who calls themself Snyde. His job provides a home beside St Oswald's but no social place within it, leaving his child close enough to observe the school while remaining decisively outside its privileged community.
characters.name: John Snyde

characters.description: A longstanding St Oswald's colleague of Straitley. Scoones belongs to the older order of the school and shares enough of its history to help define what is being lost as institutional pressures and deliberate sabotage destabilize the staff.
characters.name: Eric Scoones

recaps.ending: Straitley finally recognizes that the multiplying scandals share a deliberate source inside St Oswald's. The hidden narrator is exposed as Snyde, the porter's child who entered the school under a false identity; the narration has encouraged others to assume a male culprit, but Snyde is a woman. Her present campaign grows from childhood exclusion, her illicit access to the school, and the catastrophic end of her friendship with Leon. By the time Straitley closes in, she has exploited staff weaknesses, forged communications, and turned suspicion between colleagues, causing lasting damage even though the school itself survives. The confrontation breaks her control of the game and prevents the complete destruction she intended. Straitley, physically and professionally tested but still committed to St Oswald's, returns to his classroom. The school's traditions have proved neither innocent nor invulnerable, yet its survival gives Straitley the final advantage in the contest Snyde imagined as chess.
recaps.in_short: At the start of a new term at St Oswald's Grammar School, veteran Latin master Roy Straitley resists modernization while an unnamed new staff member begins a calculated attack from within. The saboteur, calling themself Snyde or the Black Pawn, is the child of a former school porter and has carried resentment against the elite institution since secretly entering it as a child and befriending pupil Leon Mitchell. Small thefts, forged messages, planted evidence, data breaches, and rumors accumulate into disciplinary crises and public scandal. Straitley's knowledge of the school lets him see design where others see coincidence, though the attacker repeatedly redirects suspicion. He eventually uncovers the false identity and the childhood history behind the campaign. Snyde is revealed to be a woman, overturning assumptions encouraged by her account. Her attempt to destroy St Oswald's is stopped after a final contest with Straitley, but the school and its staff have been badly shaken. Straitley survives and resumes teaching, preserving the institution without pretending it is unchanged.

recaps.text: St Oswald's begins another academic year under pressure to modernize. Roy Straitley, its veteran Latin master, distrusts the new computer systems, managerial language, and recently hired staff but remains devoted to the school. A second narrator, concealed among those newcomers, describes entering St Oswald's deliberately. Calling themself Snyde and treating the plan as a chess match, the infiltrator intends to destroy the institution from within. The campaign starts with acts small enough to be blamed on carelessness or ordinary misconduct. Because staff are already divided by status, age, and departmental rivalry, each incident creates more suspicion than its apparent importance warrants.

The hidden attacker gains access to private information and uses the school's dependence on reputation against it. Missing property, altered messages, and embarrassing disclosures make colleagues question one another. Straitley is drawn into the disturbances while also trying to protect his pupils and his place in a changing institution. In memories of childhood, Snyde recalls living beside St Oswald's as the porter's child, able to watch the boys' world but barred from belonging to it. A secret friendship with pupil Leon Mitchell offered temporary access and sharpened the pain of exclusion. The present sabotage is therefore both a planned institutional attack and a personal return to a place Snyde believes caused lasting injury.

Incidents spread beyond inconvenience into accusations capable of ending careers. Forged or manipulated evidence sends inquiries in the wrong direction, and the school's leaders respond to each crisis separately, which helps conceal the common design. Snyde studies colleagues for vulnerabilities and uses their habits as cover. Straitley notices that the pattern depends on an insider who understands both old routines and new systems. His suspicions remain difficult to prove, especially because his resistance to administrative change allows others to dismiss him as territorial or out of date. Meanwhile, the account of Snyde and Leon moves toward the childhood event that transformed envy and longing into revenge.

St Oswald's begins to fracture under public and internal pressure. Parents, governors, and staff react to scandal, while Snyde encourages the belief that several unrelated people are responsible. Straitley becomes both investigator and target. Details from the school's past allow him to test the stories surrounding the new staff, and he starts to understand that the attacker is performing an identity rather than merely hiding misconduct. The past narrative shows how Snyde's unauthorized life inside the school and bond with Leon ended in disaster, leaving St Oswald's as the object onto which grief, humiliation, and anger were fixed.

Straitley connects the present attacks with the former porter's child and narrows the possible infiltrator. Snyde responds by accelerating the campaign and turning institutional procedures against the people trying to stop it. The apparent identity of the narrator remains a weapon: colleagues and readers are encouraged to make assumptions about which new teacher is speaking. With reputations already damaged, Straitley has little room for error. The conflict becomes a direct contest between Snyde's carefully prepared false history and Straitley's memory of St Oswald's people and places.

Straitley exposes the infiltrator as Snyde, the former porter's child, and the narrative's central disguise becomes clear: Snyde is a woman who has relied on a false identity and on others' assumption that the vengeful voice belonged to a man. Her sabotage has included forged communications, planted evidence, manipulated data, and carefully directed suspicion, all rooted in her childhood exclusion and the loss connected with Leon Mitchell. The final confrontation prevents her from completing the destruction of St Oswald's, although the campaign leaves real damage behind. Straitley endures the physical and professional strain and returns to teaching. The school survives the scandal, giving him the decisive outcome in the chess game Snyde believed she controlled, while the exposure of its divisions prevents any simple restoration of the old order.

characters.description: An eight-year-old boy living on a farm with his parents and grandmother. Left alone to give Grandma her regular medicine, he decides to replace it with a concoction of his own in the hope of changing her unpleasant behavior.
characters.name: George Kranky

characters.description: George's elderly maternal grandmother, who lives with the Kranky family. She orders George about, complains constantly, and frightens him with claims about strange powers and habits. Her scheduled spoonful of brown medicine gives George the opportunity for his experiment.
characters.name: Grandma

characters.description: George's mother and Grandma's daughter. Before leaving to shop, she tells George to remain at home and give Grandma her medicine at the proper time, trusting him with what appears to be a simple household task.
characters.name: Mrs. Kranky

characters.description: George's father, a farmer with an intense interest in making his livestock larger. When he sees the extraordinary growth caused by George's mixture, he immediately thinks of its agricultural possibilities and presses George to reproduce it.
characters.name: Mr. Kranky

characters.description: A farmyard hen chosen by George as the first test subject after Grandma's transformation. A small dose makes the bird grow to an enormous size, demonstrating that the mixture affects animals as dramatically as people.
characters.name: The Brown Hen

recaps.ending: Mr. Kranky insists that George reproduce the original growth medicine for use on farm animals, but George cannot remember every ingredient or quantity. Three new mixtures produce different and impractical effects. The fourth does the reverse of the first: anything that drinks it becomes smaller. Grandma, still demanding more medicine, mistakes this batch for her usual dose and drinks it before George can stop her. She shrinks rapidly, becomes too small to see, and finally disappears altogether. Mrs. Kranky is initially shocked at the loss of her mother, while Mr. Kranky accepts the outcome with relief. George is left contemplating the unsettling result of an experiment that began as a plan to alter Grandma and grew beyond anything he could control. No usable formula for the original marvelous medicine survives.
recaps.in_short: Eight-year-old George Kranky is left to give medicine to his bullying grandmother. Hoping to transform her, he empties a wide range of household substances into a saucepan, boils the mixture, and pours it into her medicine bottle. One spoonful makes Grandma shoot upward until she is taller than the house. The medicine also makes farm animals gigantic, exciting George's farmer father, who wants the formula reproduced. George cannot remember the exact recipe, and three attempted replacements cause odd, unusable forms of growth. A fourth mixture causes shrinking instead. Grandma drinks it by mistake and dwindles until she vanishes. The original growth formula is lost, the agricultural scheme fails, and the Kranky family is left without Grandma.

recaps.text: George Kranky is left at home with his hostile grandmother while his mother goes shopping. Grandma belittles him, makes alarming claims about what elderly people can do, and orders him to bring her regular brown medicine at eleven o'clock. George decides that an ordinary dose will not improve her. Moving through the house, garage, and farm shed, he combines soaps, cosmetics, cleaning products, animal remedies, paint, and other substances, taking care not to use the medicines reserved for his parents. He heats the mixture in a large saucepan until it resembles Grandma's usual medicine, cools it, and fills the familiar bottle. The result is not a real treatment but an unpredictable experiment assembled from whatever George can find.

At medicine time, George gives Grandma a spoonful of his new mixture. She heats up, bursts upward from her chair, and grows through the ceilings and roof until her upper body towers over the house. George is alarmed but also fascinated that his invention has worked so dramatically. When he tests the remaining mixture on a chicken, the bird grows to an extraordinary size as well. The effect is therefore not unique to Grandma and appears capable of transforming the farm's animals.

George gives measured doses to more farm animals, including pigs, cattle, sheep, a pony, and a goat, and each becomes gigantic. His parents return to find both the livestock and Grandma enormously enlarged. Because Grandma is still protruding through the roof, Mr. Kranky brings in a crane to lift her out of the house. Far from being disturbed by the experiment, he is thrilled by the possibility of producing huge animals and vastly more food. He demands that George make another batch so the effect can be repeated and exploited on the farm. George explains that he did not record the many ingredients, but his father insists that they reconstruct the formula together.

George and Mr. Kranky try repeatedly to recreate the marvelous medicine. Because the original was improvised, every missed ingredient or altered amount changes the result. The second mixture produces excessive long-legged growth, the third creates another distorted form, and neither gives Mr. Kranky the useful giant animals he wants. Their fourth attempt has the opposite effect: a chicken that samples it becomes smaller. Before George can explain, Grandma demands her medicine and swallows a spoonful of this shrinking batch. She dwindles rapidly from adult size to a tiny figure and then disappears completely. Mrs. Kranky is shocked, but Mr. Kranky soon treats Grandma's absence as a benefit. The family never recovers the successful formula, and George is left wondering at the strange power his unrepeatable experiment released.

characters.description: A twenty-one-year-old mechanic who arrives in the Montsou mining district hungry and unemployed after losing a railway job for striking a superior. Intelligent, proud, and susceptible to violent anger, he has no mining experience but accepts dangerous underground work and begins learning both the trade and the grievances of the workers around him.
characters.name: Étienne Lantier

characters.description: An elderly cart driver whose given name is Vincent Maheu. After roughly half a century in and around the mines, coal dust has permanently damaged his lungs and blackened his saliva. His nickname, suggesting repeated escapes from death, reflects the industry's long claim on his body.
characters.name: Vincent Maheu

characters.description: A respected coal hewer at Le Voreux and the principal wage earner in a household spanning three generations. Competent, patient, and initially cautious about conflict with the company, he helps Étienne obtain work when the mine crew is short-handed.
characters.name: Maheu

characters.description: Maheu's wife, who manages a crowded home in the miners' settlement and stretches the family's inadequate earnings across food, rent, and many children. Practical and formidable, she understands both the household's dependence on the mine and the impossibility of sustaining it on wages that never cover its needs.
characters.name: La Maheude

characters.description: The Maheus' fifteen-year-old daughter, whose slight build and cropped appearance initially lead Étienne to mistake her for a boy. She works underground pushing coal tubs to support the household and moves through the mine with the competence of someone employed there since childhood.
characters.name: Catherine Maheu

characters.description: A strong, experienced miner in Maheu's crew. He quickly recognizes Étienne's interest in Catherine and asserts his own claim on her with possessive confidence, making personal rivalry part of the newcomers' already difficult adjustment underground.
characters.name: Chaval

characters.description: The eldest Maheu son, a miner who already has a child with Philomène. Irreverent and pleasure-seeking outside work, he nevertheless shares the dangerous occupation on which his extended family depends.
characters.name: Zacharie Maheu

characters.description: A younger Maheu son employed underground as a trapper. Small, unruly, and accustomed to neglect, he moves freely through the settlement and mine with other children who have learned adult vices alongside the demands of labor.
characters.name: Jeanlin Maheu

characters.description: A former miner dismissed for political agitation who now runs the Avantage tavern near Le Voreux. Familiar with socialist arguments and local grievances, he offers Étienne food, information, and a gathering place while favoring gradual organization over impulsive confrontation.
characters.name: Rasseneur

characters.description: A Russian émigré and skilled mechanic who lodges at Rasseneur's tavern. Quiet in daily life but uncompromising in his anarchism, he rejects reform and political organization, believing that the existing social order must be destroyed before anything new can grow.
characters.name: Souvarine

characters.description: The general manager of the Montsou mines, responsible for representing the company to workers and shareholders. Although materially comfortable, he feels trapped between remote owners, labor unrest, and an unhappy private household, and he approaches the miners chiefly through the demands of his office.
characters.name: Hennebeau

characters.description: A young mining engineer and Hennebeau's nephew, charged with supervising operations underground. Technically capable and accustomed to authority, he deals directly with crews over safety, output, and discipline.
characters.name: Paul Négrel

characters.description: A wealthy shareholder whose family fortune rests partly on the Montsou mines. He regards inherited ownership as prudent stewardship and lives at La Piolaine, largely insulated from the physical conditions that produce his income.
characters.name: Léon Grégoire

characters.description: The Grégoires' sheltered daughter and sole heir. Generous within the narrow charitable habits taught by her parents, she knows mining families mainly as recipients of visits and gifts rather than as workers tied to the source of her comfort.
characters.name: Cécile Grégoire

characters.description: An independent mine owner struggling to keep the Jean-Bart pit competitive against the larger Montsou company. More directly exposed to financial failure than the Grégoire shareholders, he still depends on extracting labor from miners facing the same dangers and scarcity.
characters.name: Deneulin

characters.description: A young mine worker from the settlement, known for her open sexuality and rough humor. She is attracted to Étienne and takes part in the communal life of the miners without sharing Catherine's reserve.
characters.name: Mouquette

recaps.ending: After the defeated miners return to work, Souvarine secretly sabotages Le Voreux. Water and unstable ground overwhelm the shaft, destroying the mine and trapping workers below. Négrel directs a long rescue effort; Zacharie dies during it. Étienne, Catherine, and Chaval remain cut off underground, where Étienne kills Chaval in a final fight. Catherine dies beside Étienne before rescuers reach him. Elsewhere, the mentally damaged Bonnemort strangles the visiting Cécile Grégoire. The catastrophe ends Deneulin's remaining independence and devastates the district without changing the system that made the strike. Étienne recovers and leaves Montsou for Paris, intending to continue political work. Maheude, now responsible for the surviving children, goes back underground because the family must eat. As Étienne walks through the spring countryside, he imagines the workers' suppressed anger as new growth beneath the soil: the strike has failed in the immediate sense, but collective resistance has taken root and will return.
recaps.in_short: Unemployed mechanic Étienne Lantier arrives at Montsou and joins the Maheu family underground at Le Voreux. Appalled by dangerous work and chronic hunger, he studies socialism and helps organize a strike after the mining company effectively cuts wages. The stoppage spreads, but the workers' small relief fund collapses and starvation divides them. A march across the district turns destructive; shopkeeper Maigrat dies, and soldiers later fire on a crowd, killing Maheu, Mouquette, and others. The survivors return to work defeated. The anarchist Souvarine then sabotages Le Voreux, causing a catastrophic flood and collapse. Trapped with Catherine and her abusive partner Chaval, Étienne kills Chaval, but Catherine dies before Étienne is rescued. Zacharie also dies in the rescue effort, while Bonnemort kills the sheltered heiress Cécile Grégoire. Maheude returns to mining to feed her remaining children. Étienne leaves for Paris convinced that, although this strike failed, the workers' shared consciousness is growing toward a future uprising.

recaps.text: Étienne Lantier reaches the Montsou coal district on a freezing night after losing his railway job. At Le Voreux he meets the elderly miner Bonnemort, whose damaged lungs embody a lifetime of coal work, and learns that the Maheu crew needs a hand. The Maheu household already sends several members underground to meet debts that continually exceed its wages. Étienne takes the vacant job and descends with Maheu, fifteen-year-old Catherine, Chaval, and the others. He is shocked by heat, darkness, water, cramped seams, and the constant possibility of collapse. Catherine teaches him to handle the coal tubs, and his attraction to her provokes the possessive Chaval. Above ground, company rules and deductions leave the workers responsible for hazards they cannot control. Étienne completes the punishing shift and finds temporary help at Rasseneur's tavern, where the former miner and the Russian anarchist Souvarine represent different forms of opposition to the company. With no better option, Étienne commits himself to mining.

Étienne settles into the district and gains skill underground, eventually lodging with the Maheus. Their home in the company settlement is crowded, hungry, and completely dependent on the wages of adults and children. Across the district, the Grégoire family receives steady income from inherited mine shares and practices charity without questioning the arrangement that protects its comfort. Manager Hennebeau and engineer Négrel administer production while independent owner Deneulin struggles to keep his own pits profitable. Catherine becomes involved with Chaval, whose jealousy and violence deepen Étienne's resentment. At the Avantage, Étienne reads political works and debates Rasseneur and Souvarine. He begins corresponding with the socialist organizer Pluchart and promotes an international workers' association, hoping that a relief fund will let miners withstand a future dispute. His education and confidence make him increasingly influential among men who recognize their hardship but fear the consequences of challenging the company.

Months of work make Étienne a trusted member of the Maheu household and a more forceful advocate of collective action. Conditions underground remain unsafe. Jeanlin is badly injured in an accident, adding another dependent to a family that cannot afford lost wages. The company, concerned about poor timbering, announces a new payment system that separates support work from coal cutting while lowering the rate paid for coal. Management presents the change as a safety reform; miners calculate that it is an effective wage reduction imposed on people already near starvation. Étienne argues that the moment has come to resist. Rasseneur doubts the workers can survive a prolonged stoppage, and Souvarine dismisses limited wage demands as inadequate, but anger spreads through the settlements. Delegates from the crews meet and vote not to return underground. The strike begins with only a modest fund, uncertain outside support, and no guarantee that all pits or families will remain united.

The strike closes Le Voreux and other pits. Maheu and selected delegates present the miners' case to Hennebeau, but the manager refuses to restore the old terms and insists that the company cannot negotiate under pressure. Étienne becomes the strike's public leader, urging solidarity and promising support from the wider socialist movement. The available money quickly disappears. Families sell possessions, incur fresh debt, and divide scraps of food; Maigrat, the local shopkeeper, uses credit and sexual coercion to exploit their desperation. Some miners begin questioning Étienne, while Rasseneur's more cautious influence returns. Pluchart visits and speaks at a large meeting, linking the local dispute to international labor organization. The miners vote to continue despite hunger. Catherine remains with Chaval, who breaks with the strike and takes work at Deneulin's Jean-Bart pit. The conflict now extends beyond a single wage schedule: it has become a test of whether workers scattered across competing mines can act as one body longer than their families can endure without pay.

Hunger and frustration turn the stoppage into a moving confrontation. A crowd led largely by the miners' women marches from pit to pit, forcing work to stop and attacking machinery associated with continued production. At Jean-Bart, Catherine is caught between Chaval, the strikers, and Étienne; Deneulin can neither protect his operation nor persuade the crowd that destroying it will improve their position. The march grows more volatile as it crosses the district. Hennebeau sees the mass approach while dealing with the collapse of his own domestic life, and the authorities prepare troops to defend company property. The crowd reaches Maigrat's shop. Trying to escape across a roof, the shopkeeper falls and is killed; women who remember his abuses mutilate his body. The day's violence fractures public sympathy and gives the company grounds for greater repression. It also reveals that Étienne, despite his leadership, cannot direct the rage released by weeks of deprivation. The strike continues, but its participants are exhausted, divided, and increasingly surrounded by force.

Soldiers occupy the mining sites while hunger reduces the strikers' ability to hold together. Jeanlin, living partly apart from his family in an underground refuge, kills a young sentry without a political or practical purpose, another sign that violence has escaped organized control. The company brings in replacement workers under military protection. A crowd gathers at Le Voreux, insulting the newcomers and confronting the troops with stones and threats. When the soldiers fire, Maheu, Mouquette, and other miners and family members are killed or wounded. The deaths destroy the remaining momentum of the strike. Hennebeau offers concessions that do not amount to victory, and workers begin returning underground because their households have no food. Étienne is blamed both by those who followed him and by authorities who see him as an agitator. He has lost his leadership, the strike fund, and his faith that a single burst of solidarity could overcome the company's resources. Le Voreux resumes production under the same broad system the miners had challenged.

As defeated miners return to Le Voreux, Souvarine acts on his belief that only destruction can clear the way for change. He secretly damages the mine's shaft system, allowing water and unstable ground to overwhelm it. The works collapse, killing workers and trapping others below. Négrel leads a prolonged rescue effort, during which Zacharie dies. Étienne, Catherine, and Chaval remain isolated in flooded passages. Étienne kills Chaval during a final fight, but Catherine weakens and dies beside him before rescuers break through. Étienne is eventually brought out alive. At the Maheu home, the mentally damaged Bonnemort strangles Cécile Grégoire when she visits, bringing the violence of the mines into direct contact with the sheltered shareholder family. Maheude, widowed and responsible for surviving children, must return to underground work. Étienne recovers and leaves Montsou for Paris to continue organizing. Walking through the spring fields, he believes the failed strike has nevertheless planted a durable consciousness among the workers and that a larger uprising will eventually emerge.
